Rout

/ROWT/ · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Rout means an overwhelming, decisive defeat — especially one that ends in a disorderly, chaotic retreat.

The invasion collapsed into a rout when the panicked soldiers threw down their shields and fled in every direction.

Worked Example

By halftime the score was 62 to 18, and the championship game everyone expected to be close had become a rout.

A rout is not just a loss but a lopsided collapse. The enormous halftime gap shows the contest stopped being competitive at all — one side has fallen apart completely.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

drubbing: A drubbing is a one-sided beating, usually on a scoreboard — the losing team takes its lumps and goes home. A rout adds collapse: the losing side comes apart, its order dissolving into flight. Every rout would count as a drubbing; not every drubbing has the panic.

trouncing: A trouncing is a thorough, overwhelming defeat, and the word watches the winner — how completely they dominated. A rout watches the loser: the moment resistance stops being resistance, lines break, and everyone runs. You trounce an opponent who keeps playing; you rout one who falls apart.

shellacking: Shellacking is the informal, joking word for a decisive, humiliating loss — talk-radio and locker-room language. Rout is the standard word that military historians and sportswriters share, and it carries a precise image the slang lacks: a side so beaten it scatters in disorder.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

triumph: a great, decisive victory

rally: a comeback surge that turns a contest around

Where it sits · how total the loss is — defeat → rout → annihilation

defeat vs. rout: A defeat can be narrow and hard-fought, but a rout is so one-sided that the losing side simply falls apart.

annihilation vs. rout: A rout scatters the losing side in disorder; an annihilation implies it was wiped out completely.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — rout

Root — rout: from Latin rupta, 'broken (company)', from rumpere, 'to break'

Put it together

Put it together: Rout comes from Latin rupta — a 'broken' company of soldiers, from rumpere, 'to break.' A rout is exactly that: the moment a force breaks apart and scatters.

Use the root in a new word: bankrupt

Use the root in a new word: bankrupt: The shop went bankrupt — a word that literally means 'broken bench,' from the same Latin root for 'break.'

Root Check

Word Choice

Journalism & history

Rout is a favorite of sportswriters and military historians. It also works as a verb: 'the champions routed their rivals.' Don't confuse it with route (a path or way) — one letter apart, completely unrelated meaning.
